title: How Landslides Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain landslides and related mass movements, prompted by a deadly 2014 landslide in Washington State near Seattle (the Steelhead Landslide area). They cover mass movement categories (creep, slump, slide, flow), the role of water, weathering versus erosion, mechanical and chemical weathering, triggers such as earthquakes, wildfires, and volcanoes (pyroclastic flows, lahars), and historical disasters including Mount St. Helens, Thistle, Utah, Lake Peigneur, the 1920 Haiyuan earthquake landslide in China, and the 1999 Vargas mudslide in Venezuela. They close with human causes like road building and deforestation, mitigation methods, and a listener mail letter from an Alaska gardener.

segments.title: Opening banter and 2014 Washington landslide news
segments.summary: The hosts open the show and discuss the recent deadly Washington landslide north of Seattle, the death toll, the missing, and the warnings the area had received.

segments.title: Mass movements and types of movement
segments.summary: Landslides are a type of mass movement, in which gravity moves soil or sediment downslope when friction is overcome. The hosts describe creep, slump, slide, and flow, and how water often causes them.

segments.title: Weathering versus erosion
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish weathering, which breaks material down, from erosion, which transports it. They explain mechanical versus chemical weathering and the five agents of erosion.

segments.title: Triggers: water, earthquakes, wildfires, volcanoes
segments.summary: The hosts list common landslide triggers: heavy rain and water saturation, earthquakes, wildfires that destroy vegetation roots, and volcanic activity including pyroclastic flows and lahars.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Message break before the discussion of triggers continues.

segments.title: Historic landslide disasters and secondary floods
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Mount St. Helens landslide, the Thistle, Utah landslide that dammed the Spanish Fork River, submarine landslides and tsunamis, the Lake Peigneur disaster, and the 1920 China landslide and 1999 Vargas mudslide.

segments.title: Human causes and mitigation
segments.summary: The hosts note that road building and deforestation can make slopes unstable, and mention mitigation such as drainage pipes, retaining walls, and reforestation. They also note landslides are often not covered by homeowners insurance.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener from Juneau, Alaska writes about listening to the show while living alone. The hosts close with social media and website information.
